part_title: GenAI Caching and Durable Agent State with ElastiCache and MemoryDB

scenes.title: ElastiCache for low-latency GenAI
scenes.narration: This is a cache-aside pattern for a GenAI response. The application first checks ElastiCache for a valid cached entry derived from the request and its relevant context. A cache hit returns an existing response quickly without paying again for retrieval and inference. On a miss, the application retrieves needed knowledge, invokes the model, then stores a suitable response with a time-to-live before returning it. The diagram shows an example hit-rate dashboard and one-hour TTL, but these are illustrative targets, not universal values. The hardest part of caching a model answer is correctness. The cache key must distinguish tenants, authorisation scope, model or prompt revision, relevant retrieved-document version and other inputs that affect the answer. Invalidate or refresh entries when source information changes. Avoid caching secrets or private conversations into broadly shared keys. A high hit rate is useful only if cached results remain accurate and authorised. Monitor hit ratio alongside latency, cost and stale-answer incidents to make sure caching improves the real user experience.

scenes.title: MemoryDB: durable in-memory state
scenes.narration: The comparison contrasts an ephemeral cache with a durable in-memory database for an AI agent. A simple cache can hold recent session details with excellent access speed, but if its data is evicted or lost during a failure, the agent may need to reconstruct the conversation and its intermediate plan. On the right, Amazon MemoryDB uses a Redis-compatible in-memory data model with durability and multi-Availability Zone replication, designed for application state that must survive failures. The illustration shows an agent writing a session and plan using hash operations and transactions. Following a node failure, a replica can be promoted and the agent can resume from retained state. Be careful with the caption implying zero data loss: real recovery guarantees depend on the service's durability model, write acknowledgement and failure scenario. MemoryDB isn't simply a more expensive ElastiCache for every workload. Use a cache when data is disposable and recoverable; use a durable database when session state or workflow progress has business value. Still implement expiry, access control and safe replay semantics for agent operations.
